gaps.sentence: Passengers ___ open the doors before the train stops completely.
gaps.hint: a safety rule that forbids something

gaps.sentence: After three attempts, she ___ pass her driving test at last.
gaps.explanation: A specific past success takes 'was able to' or 'managed to': was able to pass.

gaps.sentence: You ___ better book now — the prices rise every week.
gaps.explanation: 'Had better' gives strong advice, often with urgency: had better book.

gaps.sentence: If you want a refund, you ___ keep the receipt — no receipt, no refund.
gaps.hint: a necessity that applies in the future
gaps.explanation: Future necessity uses 'will have to': will have to keep.

gaps.sentence: When I was a child, I ___ stay up late on New Year's Eve.
gaps.hint: permission that existed in the past
gaps.explanation: 'Was allowed to' expresses past permission; 'could' is also possible: was allowed to.

gaps.sentence: ___ you swim when you were four years old?
gaps.explanation: 'Could' asks about past ability: Could you swim.

gaps.sentence: Judging by the empty plates, the food ___ have been delicious.
gaps.hint: a confident past conclusion from evidence
gaps.explanation: 'Must have' expresses a logical conclusion about the past: must have been.

gaps.sentence: You ___ have worried — everything turned out fine.
gaps.hint: the worry was unnecessary in the end
gaps.explanation: 'Needn't have' means the action happened but was unnecessary: needn't have.
